title: Linguistics
description: How language is built, used, learned and changed: sounds, words, sentences, meaning, use, change, acquisition and variation, ending with a data puzzle in which you work out a language from examples.
audience: A capable adult who speaks English well and has never studied linguistics. They know basic grammar words (noun, verb) from school.
outcomes: You'll be able to describe a consonant by place, manner and voicing.
You'll be able to find phonemes with minimal pairs and state a sound rule.
You'll be able to divide a word into morphemes and a sentence into constituents.
You'll be able to tell an entailment from an implicature.
You'll be able to use regular sound correspondences to relate languages and read a child's error as rule learning.
You'll be able to work out a pattern from data in an unfamiliar language.

modules.title: Language and its sounds
modules.summary: What a linguist is describing, how speech sounds are made, and how a language organises them into a small set of contrasts.

modules.title: Words and sentences
modules.summary: How words are built from parts, how words group into phrases, and how languages differ in how they order them.

modules.title: Meaning and use
modules.summary: What a sentence means as a matter of its words and structure, and what a speaker conveys by saying it in a context.

modules.title: Change, learning and society
modules.summary: How languages change in regular ways, how children acquire one, how it varies across speakers, and a data puzzle that uses everything.

lessons.title: What linguists describe
lessons.objective: Tell a descriptive claim from a prescriptive one and give the properties that make a human language open-ended.

concepts.title: Descriptive
concepts.summary: Stating what speakers actually say and accept, without ranking it as right or wrong.

concepts.title: Prescriptive
concepts.summary: Stating what speakers ought to say, according to a rule set by an authority.

concepts.title: Arbitrariness
concepts.summary: The link between a word's sound and its meaning is set by convention and not by resemblance.

misconceptions: Thinking grammar means the rules taught at school, so that a spoken pattern is 'ungrammatical' if a teacher would mark it.
Assuming writing is the real language and speech a poor copy.
Confusing a sentence that is odd in meaning with one that is ill-formed.
sequence: Open on three sentences: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously', 'Furiously sleep ideas green colorless' and 'The cat sat on the mat'; ask which a speaker of English accepts.
Separate form from meaning: the first is well-formed and senseless, the second is not well-formed.
Distinguish the two ways of talking about rules: describing what speakers do and saying what they should do.
Show arbitrariness with three words for the same animal (dog, chien, Hund) and show productivity by building a sentence no one has said.
Say what a grammar is for a linguist: a description of what a speaker knows.
examples: Chomsky used 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' in Syntactic Structures in 1957 to show that grammaticality and meaning come apart. 'Who did you see?' and 'Whom did you see?' are both used; a descriptive claim says which are used and where, a prescriptive claim says which should be.

figures.shows: Three cases, each a short sentence shown with its parts labelled by role (subject, verb, object); the third has its words scrambled. Role labels appear after the learner sorts.
figures.learnerAction: Sort the sentences into 'accepted' and 'not accepted' by an English speaker.

questionPlan.sample: 'Speakers of this dialect say "I seen it" in casual speech.' This claim is:
Which of these is well-formed but meaningless?
choices: The cat sat on the mat

questionPlan.sample: 'You should never end a sentence with a preposition.' This claim is:

historyNotes: Chomsky, Syntactic Structures, 1957, the colorless green ideas sentence.

lessons.title: Making speech sounds
lessons.objective: Describe a consonant by place, manner and voicing and tell how many sounds, as opposed to letters, a word has.

concepts.title: Place of articulation
concepts.summary: Where in the mouth the airflow is narrowed or blocked: lips (bilabial), teeth and lip (labiodental), tongue ridge (alveolar), soft palate (velar).

concepts.title: Manner of articulation
concepts.summary: How the airflow is shaped: a full stop of air (stop), a narrow channel (fricative) or air through the nose (nasal).

concepts.title: Voicing
concepts.summary: Whether the vocal folds vibrate during the sound.

misconceptions: Counting letters as sounds: 'ship' has four letters and three sounds.
Believing the letter 'c' always stands for one sound.
Thinking voicing is the same as loudness.
sequence: Put a finger on the throat, say /s/ and then /z/, and feel the difference in vibration: that is voicing.
Show that /p b/, /t d/, /k g/ are pairs that differ only in voicing and are produced at the lips, the tongue ridge and the soft palate.
Add manner: stops against fricatives (/s z f v/) and nasals (/m n/).
Read a consonant off the three features.
Compare sounds and letters in 'ship', 'knight' and 'box'.
examples: /p/ is a voiceless bilabial stop; /b/ is a voiced bilabial stop; /t/ is a voiceless alveolar stop; /z/ is a voiced alveolar fricative; /k/ is a voiceless velar stop. 'ship' is /ʃɪp/ (3 sounds, 4 letters); 'knight' is /naɪt/ (3 sounds, 6 letters); 'box' is /bɒks/ (4 sounds, 3 letters).

figures.shows: A side view of the vocal tract with the lips, tongue ridge, soft palate and vocal folds labelled, and a table of consonants by place, manner and voicing. The sound being described is only revealed after the learner chooses features.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a place, manner and voicing and hear the sound; then name a given sound by its features.

questionPlan.sample: /s/ and /z/ differ in one feature. Which (place, manner or voicing)?
What is the place of articulation of /k/?
How many sounds are in the word 'knight', /naɪt/?

lessons.title: Contrasts, phonemes and sound rules
lessons.objective: Find phonemes by minimal pairs and state a sound rule such as the English plural.

concepts.title: Phoneme
concepts.summary: A sound that distinguishes words in a language, such as /p/ and /b/ in 'pat' and 'bat'.

concepts.title: Allophone
concepts.summary: One of the different pronunciations of a phoneme that never distinguishes words in the language.

concepts.title: Minimal pair
concepts.summary: Two words that differ in exactly one sound and have different meanings.

misconceptions: Believing that a difference we can hear must matter to a language; aspiration of /p/ is audible but does not change a word in English.
Thinking spelling shows how a plural sounds: 'dogs' ends in /z/.
Treating a rule as a list of memorised forms.
sequence: Start with 'pat' and 'bat': one sound changes the meaning, so /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes.
Hold a piece of paper to the lips for 'pin' and 'spin': the p in 'pin' puffs out air (aspirated), the p in 'spin' does not, yet speakers hear one sound.
Say that aspirated and unaspirated p are allophones of /p/ because they occur in different places.
State the plural rule: /s/ after voiceless sounds, /z/ after voiced sounds, /ɪz/ after sibilants.
Test it on new words.
examples: cats /kæts/ (/s/), dogs /dɒɡz/ (/z/), buses /bʌsɪz/ (/ɪz/), books (/s/), cabs (/z/), dishes (/ɪz/). Minimal pairs: pat/bat, ship/chip, sip/zip.

figures.shows: Word lists with the final sound of each noun marked, and a column for the plural ending the learner chooses.
figures.learnerAction: Complete the plural column by choosing /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/.

questionPlan.sample: What is the plural ending sound in 'dogs': /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/?
What is the plural ending sound in 'books'?
Which pair is a minimal pair?

lessons.title: Words are built from parts
lessons.objective: Divide a word into morphemes and say whether an affix is inflectional or derivational.

concepts.title: Morpheme
concepts.summary: The smallest unit of form that carries meaning or grammatical function.

concepts.title: Inflection
concepts.summary: An ending that marks a grammatical feature such as plural or past without making a new word.

concepts.title: Derivation
concepts.summary: An affix that makes a new word, often changing its category: happy to happiness.

misconceptions: Counting syllables as morphemes: 'cat' has one of each, but 'unbreakable' has three morphemes and four syllables.
Thinking every word that ends in -s is plural.
Assuming all languages build words in the same way as English.
sequence: Ask how many meaningful pieces there are in 'unbreakable': un-, break, -able.
Define free and bound morphemes.
Show the difference between inflection and derivation with -ed and -ness.
Show Turkish 'evlerimizden', ev + ler + imiz + den, house + plural + our + from, one word where English needs a phrase.
Close by noting that some languages pack a lot into a word.
examples: unbreakable = un + break + able (3). cats = cat + s (2). happiness = happy + ness (2). internationalization = inter + nation + al + ize + ation (5). Turkish evlerimizden = ev + ler + imiz + den (4), meaning 'from our houses'. -s in 'cats' is inflectional; -ness in 'happiness' is derivational.

figures.shows: Words shown as a row of coloured blocks, one per morpheme, with the glosses hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Tap the boundary marks between morphemes in each word.

questionPlan.sample: How many morphemes are in 'unbreakable'?
How many morphemes are in 'internationalization' (inter-nation-al-ize-ation)?
In 'happiness', the ending -ness is:

historyNotes: Turkish evlerimizden, 'from our houses', is a standard textbook example; check the gloss before use.

lessons.title: Words into phrases
lessons.objective: Find a sentence's constituents with substitution and movement tests, and say how one string can have two structures.

concepts.title: Constituent
concepts.summary: A group of words that works as a single unit in a sentence.

concepts.title: Phrase
concepts.summary: A constituent built around a head word, such as a noun phrase around a noun.

concepts.title: Structural ambiguity
concepts.summary: A sentence with one string of words and two structures, so two meanings.

misconceptions: Treating a sentence as a flat line of words.
Believing two readings must come from two different words.
Taking any sequence of words as a constituent.
sequence: Replace 'the small dog' in 'The small dog chased the cat' with 'it': the pronoun replaces the whole group, so it is a constituent.
Try the same with 'small dog chased': it fails, so it is not.
Show a sentence with two structures: 'I saw the man with the telescope'.
Draw the two groupings by brackets.
State what the test tells us: structure is real even though it is unseen.
examples: 'The small dog chased the cat' becomes 'It chased the cat' and 'The small dog chased it'. 'Small dog chased' cannot be replaced by a single word. 'I saw [the man with the telescope]' (the man has it) against 'I [saw the man] [with the telescope]' (I used it).

figures.shows: Case 1: a clause with parts labelled subject, verb, object. Case 2: the ambiguous sentence in two bracketings. Labels are revealed after the learner groups the words.
figures.learnerAction: Group the words into the phrases they form.
figures.placement: Constituents as the unit of syntax.

questionPlan.sample: Which can be replaced by 'it' in 'The small dog chased the cat'?
In 'I saw the man with the telescope', how many structures does the string have?
Which of these groups of words is a constituent of 'The tall girl read the book'?

lessons.title: Order, difference and recursion
lessons.objective: Describe a language's basic word order and count the levels of embedding in a sentence.

concepts.title: Basic word order
concepts.summary: The usual order of subject, object and verb in a plain declarative sentence.

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A rule that can apply to its own output, so that a phrase can sit inside a phrase of the same kind.

concepts.title: Embedding
concepts.summary: A clause placed inside another clause.

misconceptions: Assuming the English order is the natural one.
Thinking a long sentence has to be an unlimited one; recursion is about the rule.
Counting clauses as sentences.
sequence: Show 'She read the book' (SVO), a Japanese order 'Tarō ga ringo o tabeta' (Taro apple ate, SOV), and the Welsh verb-first order.
State that SOV and SVO are the two most common orders in the world's languages and that this is tallied in WALS.
Build 'the cat that chased the rat that ate the malt' by adding a clause at a time.
Count levels and show that the rule has no limit in principle.
Distinguish what a speaker can do from what the rule allows.
examples: 'Tarō ga ringo o tabeta': Taro (S) apple (O) ate (V), so SOV. 'This is the malt. This is the rat that ate the malt. This is the cat that chased the rat that ate the malt' has two embedded relative clauses in the last sentence.

figures.shows: Case 1: English clause with S, V, O labelled. Case 2: Japanese clause labelled S, O, V. Case 3: a sentence with two relative clauses shown nested.
figures.learnerAction: Reorder the labelled parts into each language's basic order; then count the nested clauses.

questionPlan.sample: What is the basic order of Japanese 'Tarō ga ringo o tabeta' (Taro apple ate): SVO, SOV or VSO?
'The cat that chased the rat that ate the malt': how many relative clauses are embedded?
A rule that allows a clause inside a clause of the same kind is called:

historyNotes: Check WALS for the figures on basic word order before quoting numbers.

lessons.title: What a sentence entails
lessons.objective: Use entailment to compare sentences and say how sense differs from reference.

concepts.title: Entailment
concepts.summary: Sentence A entails B if B must be true whenever A is true.

concepts.title: Compositionality
concepts.summary: The meaning of a sentence is built from the meanings of its parts and how they are combined.

concepts.title: Sense and reference
concepts.summary: Reference is the thing a phrase picks out; sense is the way it picks it out.

misconceptions: Treating anything one infers from a sentence as an entailment.
Thinking active and passive sentences mean different things because they sound different.
Thinking two phrases with the same reference mean the same.
sequence: Define entailment with a test: if A is true, can B be false?
Apply it to 'Mira killed the spider' and 'The spider died', and then to 'Mira swatted the spider'.
Compare active and passive: 'The dog bit the postman' and 'The postman was bitten by the dog' are true in the same situations.
Introduce hyponymy: 'It is a poodle' entails 'It is a dog', but not the reverse.
Introduce Frege's example: 'the morning star' and 'the evening star' refer to Venus but differ in sense.
examples: 'Mira killed the spider' entails 'The spider died'. 'Mira swatted the spider' does not entail it. 'It is a poodle' entails 'It is a dog', but 'It is a dog' does not entail 'It is a poodle'. Frege's 1892 paper 'Über Sinn und Bedeutung' uses the morning star and the evening star.

figures.shows: Case 1: the 'voice' model for 'the dog bit the postman', with the active and passive shown; case 2: the agentless form. The truth conditions are hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the sentence between active and passive and say whether the truth conditions change.

questionPlan.sample: 'Mira killed the spider' entails:
'The dog bit the postman' and 'The postman was bitten by the dog' are true:
choices: Only when the dog is large

questionPlan.sample: 'It is a dog' and 'It is a poodle': which entails the other?
questionPlan.answer: 'It is a poodle' entails 'It is a dog'
choices: 'It is a dog' entails 'It is a poodle'
'It is a poodle' entails 'It is a dog'

lessons.title: What a speaker conveys
lessons.objective: Separate what a sentence entails from what a speaker implicates, using Grice's maxims and the cancel test.

concepts.title: Implicature
concepts.summary: What a speaker conveys beyond what the sentence entails, by relying on the listener to assume the speaker is cooperative.

concepts.title: Maxim
concepts.summary: One of Grice's four expectations of a cooperative speaker: say enough (Quantity), say what you believe true (Quality), be relevant (Relation), be clear (Manner).

concepts.title: Speech act
concepts.summary: An action done by saying something, such as promising or requesting.

misconceptions: Treating everything a hearer infers as part of the sentence's meaning.
Believing implicature is lying.
Taking 'Can you pass the salt?' as a question about ability.
sequence: Start with 'Some of the students passed' and ask what a hearer concludes: that not all did.
Ask whether it is entailed: add 'in fact, all of them' and the speaker has not contradicted themselves, so it is not.
Introduce Grice's cooperative principle and the maxim of Quantity as the reason.
Introduce speech acts: 'I promise to call' does something; 'Can you pass the salt?' requests.
Add deixis: 'I', 'here' and 'now' depend on context.
examples: 'Some of the students passed' entails that at least one passed and implicates that not all did; 'Some passed, in fact all did' is consistent, which shows the implicature can be cancelled. 'Can you pass the salt?' is a request, not a question about ability.

figures.shows: Two columns, 'entailed' and 'implicated', with sentences to sort. The cancel test result is hidden until the learner tries it.
figures.learnerAction: Add a cancelling phrase to each sentence and say whether it still holds.

questionPlan.sample: 'Some of the students passed' normally implicates that:
Which can be cancelled without contradiction?
questionPlan.answer: The implicature that not all passed
choices: The entailment that at least one passed
The implicature that not all passed

questionPlan.sample: Grice's maxim that asks speakers to say as much as needed and no more is called what?

historyNotes: Grice, Logic and Conversation, 1975; Austin, How to Do Things with Words, 1962 (lectures given at Harvard in 1955).

lessons.title: How languages change
lessons.objective: Use regular sound correspondences between cognates to predict a form and place stages of English in order.

concepts.title: Cognate
concepts.summary: A word in two languages that descends from one word in their common ancestor.

concepts.title: Sound change
concepts.summary: A regular shift in how a sound is pronounced, which affects every word with the sound in the same position.

concepts.title: Language family
concepts.summary: A group of languages descended from one ancestor, such as Indo-European.

misconceptions: Thinking a language becomes 'corrupted' as it changes.
Believing words are similar by chance or by borrowing only.
Expecting a sound change to apply to a few words at random.
sequence: Line up Latin and English: pater/father, pes/foot, piscis/fish, tres/three, canis/hound, cornu/horn.
Read off the pattern: Latin p matches Germanic f, t matches th, k matches h.
Note that the pattern is regular, which is how Sir William Jones's 1786 remark about Sanskrit, Greek and Latin turned into the comparative method.
Use the pattern to predict a new form.
Put stages of English on a timeline: 1066, 1476, 1623, 1755.
examples: Latin pater / English father; Latin pes / English foot; Latin tres / English three; Latin canis / English hound; Latin cornu / English horn. 1066 Norman Conquest; 1476 Caxton's press at Westminster; 1623 First Folio; 1755 Johnson's Dictionary.

figures.shows: A timeline 1000 to 1800 with 1066 Norman Conquest, 1476 Caxton sets up his press, 1623 Shakespeare's First Folio, 1755 Johnson's Dictionary.
figures.learnerAction: Place the four events and see which stage of English each opens.

questionPlan.sample: Latin p matches which English sound in pater/father?
Latin t in tres matches which English sound in three?
Order: Johnson's Dictionary; the Norman Conquest; the First Folio; Caxton's press.
questionPlan.answer: Norman Conquest (1066), Caxton (1476), First Folio (1623), Johnson (1755)

historyNotes: Jones delivered his discourse to the Asiatic Society in Calcutta in 1786; check the wording before quoting.

lessons.title: How children acquire language
lessons.objective: Read a child's error as evidence of a rule and name the typical order of milestones.

concepts.title: Overregularisation
concepts.summary: Applying a rule to a word that is an exception, as in 'goed' or 'mouses'.

concepts.title: Wug test
concepts.summary: A task in which a child is shown a nonsense creature and asked to complete 'two ...', to test whether they apply a rule to a new word.

concepts.title: Milestone
concepts.summary: A typical stage reached at about a given age.

misconceptions: Treating a child's error as a failure to learn rather than as use of a rule.
Believing children learn by imitation and correction alone.
Treating milestone ages as exact.
sequence: Present a child saying 'goed' and 'mouses' and ask what must have been learned.
Explain Berko's wug test of 1958: a child who says 'wugs' has not heard the word before.
Link to phonology: the plural of 'wug' is /z/, by the same rule as in 'dogs'.
Lay out the usual milestones: babbling around six months, first words around twelve, two-word combinations around eighteen to twenty-four months.
Raise the question of how much is built in and how much is learned from input.
examples: A child says 'goed': the child has the rule 'add -ed' and applies it to an exception. 'Wug' ends in a voiced consonant, so the plural is /wʌɡz/. Typical child sequence: went, then goed, then went again.

figures.shows: A line of the proportion of correct 'went' over age for a typical child (a U shape), drawn as a schematic curve with no numeric axis, since the real data vary by child.
figures.learnerAction: Place the point on the curve where overregularisation begins.

questionPlan.sample: A child says 'mouses'. This shows the child:
questionPlan.answer: Has learned the plural rule and overapplies it
choices: Has learned the plural rule and overapplies it

questionPlan.sample: What is the sound at the end of the plural 'wugs': /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/?
Rate your recall: explain why 'goed' is evidence of rule learning, in your own words.

historyNotes: Berko 1958. Milestone ages are approximate; check against a developmental source before quoting.

lessons.title: Variation and society
lessons.objective: Tell accent from dialect and register, and read a sociolinguistic variable as evidence of social patterns.

concepts.title: Accent
concepts.summary: A way of pronouncing a language.

concepts.title: Dialect
concepts.summary: A variety of a language with its own vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation.

concepts.title: Sociolinguistic variable
concepts.summary: A feature that speakers realise in different ways depending on who they are and the setting.

misconceptions: Believing a standard variety is better in itself rather than a socially favoured one.
Treating dialects as mistakes in a standard.
Confusing accent with dialect.
sequence: Ask how a linguist would measure a social fact about speech.
Describe Labov's New York department-store study of 1962: ask for a department on 'the fourth floor' and count whether the r is pronounced.
Report the pattern: the r was pronounced more in the higher-status store and more in careful speech.
Distinguish accent, dialect, register and code-switching.
Return to prescriptive and descriptive.
examples: The three stores were Saks Fifth Avenue, Macy's and S. Klein, ranked by status. The variable was the pronunciation of /r/ after a vowel, in 'fourth floor'.

figures.shows: Three bars for the percentage of speakers using the r in each store, with values taken from Labov (1966); the writer must copy them from the source and not invent them.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the store labels onto the bars in the order you predict.
figures.placement: A social pattern in a sound.

questionPlan.sample: A difference in pronunciation only is called:
What sound did Labov count in 'fourth floor'?
Which store was ranked highest in Labov's study?

historyNotes: The quotation 'a language is a dialect with an army and a navy' is attributed to Max Weinreich (1945); check before quoting.

lessons.title: Working out a language from data
lessons.objective: Use data from one language to infer a morphological pattern and apply it to new forms.

concepts.title: Interlinear gloss
concepts.summary: A line of text with morpheme-by-morpheme meanings written beneath it.

concepts.title: Noun class
concepts.summary: A grammatical group of nouns that take the same prefixes, as in Swahili.

concepts.title: Paradigm
concepts.summary: A table of the forms of a word or of a set of words.

misconceptions: Looking for a rule in the translations alone instead of in the matching parts of the forms.
Treating each word as unrelated.
Stopping at the first pattern that fits without testing it on every form.
sequence: Give a small set of Swahili verbs with translations.
Line them up and isolate the part that changes with the subject and the part that changes with the tense.
Write the rules and test on every given form.
Generate a new form.
Add noun pairs (mtoto, watoto) for the plural pattern.
examples: Data: nimesoma 'I have read'; umesoma 'you have read'; amesoma 's/he has read'; nitasoma 'I will read'; walisoma 'they read'; tulipika 'we cooked'. Subject prefixes ni- I, u- you, a- s/he, tu- we, wa- they; tense markers -me- perfect, -ta- future, -li- past. Predict: 'we have cooked' = tumepika; 'you will read' = utasoma. Plurals: mtoto / watoto (child/children), kitabu / vitabu (book/books), mtu / watu (person/people).

figures.shows: The data set as an interlinear table with the gloss row blank for the learner to fill.
figures.learnerAction: Fill each gloss cell with the morpheme meaning.

questionPlan.sample: Using the data, how do you say 'we have cooked' in Swahili?
How do you say 'you will read'?
What is the plural of kikapu (basket), if kitabu goes to vitabu?

historyNotes: Swahili forms are standard textbook examples; a Swahili speaker or grammar should confirm each form.

courseCheck: A mixed set: name a consonant from its features; count sounds against letters; pick the minimal pair; give the plural ending sound; segment words into morphemes and classify affixes; apply a constituency test; identify basic word order and count embedding; judge entailment against implicature with the cancel test; predict a cognate from a sound correspondence; read an overregularisation; classify accent, dialect and register; and apply the Swahili pattern to a new form.
